problem_statement: Enterprise teams integrating LangChain chat model and tool providers cannot reliably configure authentication and transport security. ChatAnthropic and similar chat model integrations lack support for custom HTTP clients and mutual-TLS (mTLS), which blocks organizations that require certificate-based authentication behind corporate proxies or internal PKI. Separately, MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool discovery fails to forward auth headers/tokens consistently, causing 403 errors even when credentials are correctly configured. Provider integrations also diverge in how they manage the underlying httpx client: AzureChatOpenAI and BaseChatOpenAI do not share connection/auth setup, creating redundant connection overhead and inconsistent behavior across providers. Finally, SSRF/allowlist host validation can be bypassed via environment-based auth checks, allowing requests to untrusted hosts to slip past security validation. Together these gaps mean enterprise users cannot securely and consistently connect through proxies, custom certificates, and MCP servers without writing fragile, integration-specific workarounds.
target_user: Enterprise developers and platform engineers integrating LangChain chat model providers and MCP tool servers within organizations that enforce certificate-based authentication, corporate proxies, and strict egress/host validation policies

user_stories.persona: an enterprise developer deploying ChatAnthropic behind a corporate proxy
user_stories.action: configure a custom HTTP client with mTLS certificates
user_stories.value: I can authenticate through my organization's PKI without forking or patching the library

user_stories.persona: a developer integrating an MCP tool server
user_stories.action: have my configured auth headers/tokens reliably forwarded during tool discovery
user_stories.value: I stop getting spurious 403 errors when my credentials are actually correct

user_stories.persona: a platform engineer maintaining multiple provider integrations
user_stories.action: rely on a shared, consistent httpx client/connection-pooling layer across AzureChatOpenAI, BaseChatOpenAI, and other providers
user_stories.value: I avoid redundant connection and auth setup overhead and get predictable behavior across providers

user_stories.persona: a security engineer responsible for outbound request policy
user_stories.action: have SSRF/allowlist validation enforced consistently regardless of environment-based auth configuration
user_stories.value: untrusted hosts cannot bypass security validation through environment manipulation

acceptance_criteria.given: a user supplies a custom httpx client configured with mTLS client certificates to ChatAnthropic
acceptance_criteria.when: a request is made to the Anthropic API
acceptance_criteria.then: the request completes successfully using the provided certificate-based authentication without additional workarounds

acceptance_criteria.given: an MCP client has valid auth headers/tokens configured
acceptance_criteria.when: tool discovery is performed against an MCP server
acceptance_criteria.then: the configured headers are forwarded on every discovery request and no 403 is returned due to missing/dropped headers

acceptance_criteria.given: AzureChatOpenAI and BaseChatOpenAI are both used in the same process
acceptance_criteria.when: each provider issues requests requiring authentication
acceptance_criteria.then: both integrations reuse a shared httpx client/connection pool rather than creating redundant client instances

acceptance_criteria.given: an environment variable or auth-related config attempts to disable or bypass host allowlist validation
acceptance_criteria.when: a request is made to a host not on the allowlist
acceptance_criteria.then: the request is blocked and the SSRF validation cannot be bypassed via environment-based auth settings

acceptance_criteria.given: a developer passes a custom HTTP client to any supported chat model integration
acceptance_criteria.then: the custom client's TLS/proxy/auth settings are honored consistently, matching documented behavior across providers

acceptance_criteria.given: auth header forwarding or mTLS configuration fails
acceptance_criteria.then: the error message clearly identifies the auth/transport failure cause rather than a generic 403 or connection error

success_metrics.name: Custom client / mTLS support coverage
success_metrics.definition: count of chat model integrations (starting with ChatAnthropic) that accept a user-supplied custom httpx client supporting mTLS
success_metrics.target: all in-scope integrations (at least the 1 flagged: ChatAnthropic) support custom mTLS clients within the release

success_metrics.name: Auth-related MCP discovery failures
success_metrics.definition: count of reported issues describing 403s during MCP tool discovery despite correctly configured credentials
success_metrics.target: reduce to 0 reopened/reported instances in the two releases following the fix

success_metrics.name: Shared client adoption across providers
success_metrics.definition: count of provider integrations (AzureChatOpenAI, BaseChatOpenAI, and others) migrated to the shared httpx client/connection-pooling layer
success_metrics.target: at least 2 provider integrations migrated within the first release cycle

success_metrics.name: SSRF bypass reports
success_metrics.definition: count of confirmed reports of SSRF/allowlist bypass via environment-based auth checks after the fix ships
success_metrics.target: 0 confirmed bypass reports in the release following the fix

out_of_scope: Building a full enterprise proxy/certificate management UI or dashboard
Adding new authentication protocols (e.g., OAuth device flow, SAML) not already requested in the pain points
Rewriting MCP protocol specification or transport layer beyond header forwarding
Performance tuning of connection pooling beyond eliminating redundant client creation
Auditing or hardening authentication for providers not mentioned in the pain points

risks.description: Evidence for this theme is thin: three of the four pain points have a frequency of only 1, meaning most of this PRD rests on a single high-frequency cluster (custom HTTP client/mTLS support) and isolated individual reports rather than broad, repeated evidence.

Introducing shared httpx client/connection pooling across providers (AzureChatOpenAI, BaseChatOpenAI, etc.) risks regressions in existing auth flows that currently work, since these integrations were built independently.

Hardening SSRF/allowlist validation could break legitimate enterprise configurations that currently rely on environment-based auth checks to reach internal hosts, causing support friction if not carefully scoped.
mTLS/custom client support may vary by underlying provider SDK capabilities, meaning full parity across all chat model integrations may not be achievable in a single release.
